analysis.one_liner: Reinstates expired taxes on oil and chemical companies to fund cleanup of toxic Superfund sites.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Finance Committee without a vote, a committee hearing, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have brought back the Superfund cleanup taxes on crude oil, chemical feedstocks, and corporate profits that expired in 1995, with a temporary 50 percent surcharge from 2008 through 2012 earmarked for the largest and most dangerous contaminated sites. Since those taxes lapsed, cleanup of abandoned toxic sites has been paid by ordinary taxpayers instead of the polluting industries the program originally charged. The bill never moved after being referred to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near Superfund sites — the bill's findings note that one in four Americans lives within three miles of one — would gain faster cleanup of the largest, most severely contaminated sites and sites with uncontrolled exposure risks. Taxpayers generally would also gain, because the bill's findings state that the 1995 expiration of the industry taxes shifted cleanup costs onto the general public.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near toxic Superfund sites and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Reinstates the Hazardous Substance Superfund financing rate on crude oil and chemical feedstocks and the corporate environmental income tax whenever the Superfund trust fund balance falls below $5.7 billion, restoring a dedicated revenue stream from the industries that created hazardous substances.

Adds a 50 percent surcharge on those taxes from 2008 through 2012, with the proceeds reserved in a new account exclusively for sites expected to cost more than $50 million to clean up or that the EPA designates as posing high health risks.

Directs more money to megasites, which the bill's findings say absorbed 45 percent of Superfund construction and post-construction funds in fiscal year 2006 across only 14 sites, crowding out cleanup at other communities' sites.
Requires the EPA to report to Congress annually on the status, costs, cost overruns, and schedule of cleanup at every non-federal site on the National Priorities List.

analysis.who_pays: Crude oil producers and refiners, manufacturers of the listed chemical feedstocks, and corporations generally would pay the reinstated excise and environmental income taxes. Some of those costs would likely be passed through to consumers in the prices of fuel and chemical products. Companies found responsible for contamination would remain liable under existing law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil, chemical, and other corporate polluters

drawbacks.text: Excise taxes on oil and chemicals are largely passed through to consumers, so a portion of the cleanup funding would come from ordinary people at the gas pump and in goods prices rather than from industry profits.

The 50 percent surcharge is temporary, ending after 2012, while the bill's own findings state that many megasites — more than half of listed mining sites — will require operation and maintenance in perpetuity, so the dedicated funding does not match the timescale of the problem.
The new account can only be spent on megasites and high-risk sites, so cleanup at smaller, ordinary Superfund sites depends on the general fund mechanism rather than this dedicated money.

The tax switches off automatically whenever the trust fund balance exceeds $5.7 billion, which creates year-to-year uncertainty in revenue for a cleanup program the bill itself describes as needing decades of stable funding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would restore the original polluter-pays financing of Superfund and direct real money at the largest and most dangerous contamination, at a cost spread across oil, chemical, and corporate taxpayers — some of which would reach consumers. Its main design weakness is the mismatch between a short-term surcharge and cleanups that the bill itself says will take decades or continue forever. On balance the benefits to public health and to taxpayers, who currently absorb cleanup costs for sites with no responsible party, outweigh the costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Robert Casey introduced the bill on April 20, 2007, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action was ever taken: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action appear in the full action history.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor at any point.

The bill's findings state that the Superfund taxes expired in 1995, contributing to a funding shortfall that shifted cleanup costs to the general public and blocked new construction funding at numerous sites in fiscal years 2004 through 2006.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil refiners and chemical manufacturers came out ahead, avoiding reinstated cleanup taxes, while the general taxpayer continued to fund cleanups of orphaned toxic sites through general revenues.

for.name: Sen. Robert Casey Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Pennsylvania; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill; it received no hearing, markup, or vote and died in committee.

against.name: Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split appears anywhere in the record.

industries.industry: Crude oil producers and petroleum refiners
industries.note: The bill would have reinstated the per-barrel Superfund excise tax on crude oil plus a 50 percent surcharge; its lapse since 1995 lets the industry avoid that cost. The bill's findings say the lapse shifted cleanup costs to the general public.

The bill would have reinstated the excise tax on chemical feedstocks plus a 50 percent temporary increase, and kept the industry liable for its own releases. Avoiding the tax means cleanup of contaminated sites stays on the public's books.

The bill reinstates the 0.12 percent corporate environmental income tax, raised to 0.18 percent in 2008-2012, whenever the trust fund runs low. That is a broad but modest corporate tax whose proceeds would fund public health cleanups.
